\chapter{Overhead}
\label{ch:ta-overhead}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the sky, the sun, the moon, the stars and a cloud in Tamil.}

Complete TA-C51-cloud and say all five words in order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ākāyam]{\ta{ஆகாயம்} (ākāyam) — the sky}

\label{lesson:TA-C51-sky}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run of words: what did \emph{veṟṟilai} mean, and what did \emph{varavēṟpu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{ஆகாயம்}}
\textbf{\ta{ஆகாயம்}} (\emph{ākāyam}) — \textquotedblleft{}the sky\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{ākāśa}, the open lit space. Malayalam and Telugu both keep the \emph{ś} their letters can write and say \emph{ākāśaṁ}. Tamil has no letter for that sound, so the word arrives softened, with a \ta{ய} standing where the \emph{ś} was, and settles as \ta{ஆகாயம்}.

Tamil's own inherited word for the same overhead space is \emph{vāṉ}, which you have already met inside \emph{vāṉilai}, the weather — the standing of the sky. \ta{ஆகாயம்} took the wider and emptier sense: not the weather over your head but the space itself.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five things above you.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ākāyam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{vaṇakkam}, then \emph{ākāyam}, as you would greet somebody out of doors
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{ஆகாயம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the sky\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sūriyaṉ]{\ta{சூரியன்} (sūriyaṉ) — the sun}

\label{lesson:TA-C51-sun}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{ākāyam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{சூரியன்}}
\textbf{\ta{சூரியன்}} (\emph{sūriyaṉ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the sun\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{sūrya}, and the three sisters differ only in what they hang on the end of it. Telugu makes \te{సూర్యుడు} (\emph{sūryuḍu}), Malayalam \emph{sūryan}, Tamil \ta{சூரியன்}. The ending is the part each language owns; the sun is shared.

Tamil's inherited sun is \emph{ñāyiṟu}, the word standing behind the name of the first day of the week you already count through. It stepped back into the calendar and into poetry and left the daily sun to \ta{சூரியன்}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two: the space, and the thing that lights it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sūriyaṉ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{ākāyam}, then \emph{sūriyaṉ}, the sky first and then what is in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{சூரியன்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the sun\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nilā]{\ta{நிலா} (nilā) — the moon}

\label{lesson:TA-C51-moon}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{sūriyaṉ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நிலா}}
\textbf{\ta{நிலா}} (\emph{nilā}) — \textquotedblleft{}the moon\textquotedblright{}.

Where both sisters took the Sanskrit moon — \emph{candran} in Malayalam, \emph{candruḍu} in Telugu — Tamil's everyday moon is its own. \ta{நிலா} is inherited, and it is the moon as light rather than as a body: \emph{nilā} is what lies on a courtyard at night, the moonlight and the moon in one word. Tamil has \emph{cantiraṉ} as well, from the same Sanskrit its sisters took, and saves it for almanacs and for verse.

Let the \ta{ஆ} at the end run long. It is the length that makes the word.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three: the space, the day light, and the night one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{nilā}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{sūriyaṉ}, then \emph{nilā}, and let the second one end long
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நிலா} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the moon\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viṇmīṉ]{\ta{விண்மீன்} (viṇmīṉ) — a star}

\label{lesson:TA-C51-star}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{nilā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{விண்மீன்}}
\textbf{\ta{விண்மீன்}} (\emph{viṇmīṉ}) — \textquotedblleft{}a star\textquotedblright{}.

Two pieces, and they come apart cleanly. \emph{viṇ} is the sky as height, the open air above; \emph{mīṉ} is a fish, and from the oldest Tamil poetry onward it is a star as well. A star, in Tamil, is a fish in the sky — a shoal of small bright things moving in something you cannot walk on.

The sisters went other ways. Malayalam takes the Sanskrit \ml{നക്ഷത്രം} (\emph{nakṣatraṁ}); Telugu says \te{చుక్క} (\emph{cukka}), which is also its word for a dot.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this one is a picture rather than a name.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{viṇmīṉ}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nilā}, then \emph{viṇmīṉ}, the big light and then the small ones
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{விண்மீன்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a star\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mēkam]{\ta{மேகம்} (mēkam) — a cloud}

\label{lesson:TA-C51-cloud}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{viṇmīṉ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மேகம்}}
\textbf{\ta{மேகம்}} (\emph{mēkam}) — \textquotedblleft{}a cloud\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{megha}, taken in whole. Tamil has inherited cloud-words too — \emph{mukil} and \emph{kār}, both still alive in names and in verse — but \ta{மேகம்} is the one doing the daily work.

Telugu did not borrow here at all: its cloud is \emph{mabbu}, its own. Which words a language takes and which it keeps is rarely tidy. On the sky the two of them borrowed together; on the cloud they part.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
That is the whole sky: the space, the sun, the moon, the small lights, and the thing that hides them.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mēkam}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order — \emph{ākāyam}, \emph{sūriyaṉ}, \emph{nilā}, \emph{viṇmīṉ}, \emph{mēkam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{மேகம்} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a cloud\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
